messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Compilation error
parts:
I don't know what is the deal here, but it is a bug if a model compiles for Windows and not some other operating system.

You might try taking -fpic out of your $HOME/.R/Makevars file, as perhaps the RStan package wasn't installed under -fpic? The -pipe should be safe though.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Compilation error
parts:
The problem is that block.hpp doesn't include validate_column_index.hpp.
It's been fixed already on the develop branch.

The puzzle isn't so much why it doesn't work on some platforms, but
how it worked on any platforms.

Here's the buggy 1.3 file, which is missing an include.

src/stan/math/matrix/block.hpp
============================================================
#ifndef __STAN__MATH__MATRIX__BLOCK_HPP__
#define __STAN__MATH__MATRIX__BLOCK_HPP__

#include <stan/math/matrix/Eigen.hpp>
#include <stan/math/matrix/validate_row_index.hpp>

namespace stan {
namespace math {

/**
* Return a nrows x ncols submatrix starting at (i,j).
*
* @param m Matrix
* @param i Starting row
* @param j Starting column
* @param nrows Number of rows in block
* @param ncols Number of columns in block
**/
template <typename T>
inline
Eigen::Matrix<T,Eigen::Dynamic,Eigen::Dynamic>
block(const Eigen::Matrix<T,Eigen::Dynamic,Eigen::Dynamic>& m,
size_t i, size_t j, size_t nrows, size_t ncols) {
validate_row_index(m,i,"block");
validate_row_index(m,i+nrows-1,"block");
validate_column_index(m,j,"block");
validate_column_index(m,j+ncols-1,"block");
return m.block(i - 1,j - 1,nrows,ncols);
}

}
}
#endif

- Bob

On 8/30/13 1:12 PM, Carlos wrote:
> Thanks Bob! Also, by the way, I am a bit confused on how to use the block(matrix, i, j, n_rows, n_cols) function. The
> manual says that it,
>
> "Return the submatrix of x that starts at row i and column j and extends n_rows rows and n_cols columns."
>
> So, for example, let us suppose that I have a matrix A, which is 10x10. In Matlab, if I want a submatrix, I just write B
> = A(3:4, 5:7), for example, which ends up being a 2x3 matrix. In STAN, as long as I am correct, I should write,
>
> block(A, 3, 5, 2, 3)

Right. We followed the convention in the Eigen software
library. We hope to add the MATLAB-style low:high notation
in a future release. It actually shouldn't be too hard the
way things are abstracted now.

> Also, if I have a matrix C which just one row (1x10, for example), and I want the elements 6:10 (1x5), I would write
> block(C,1,6,1,5). Is this correct?

Yes, that's right if you have a 1 x 10 matrix.

In Stan, you should use a row-vector type for a (1 x 10) matrix.
But unfortunately, Stan 1.3 doesn't yet support the slicing
operations for vectors. In Stan 2.0, if rv is a row vector,
you can do tail(rv,5) to return the last five elements as a row
vector.

Now having said that, a loop in Stan isn't going to be any slower
than a block operation, but it won't have the error checking of
the block() or tail() operations.

If you have another reason (other than slicing) for wanting
a 1 x 10 matrix, we'd like to know why, because it may reflect
a shortcoming in the way we do type inference or the set of matrix
operations we support.

- Bob
